quote: However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed.

claim: In ISS concurrent-flow tests on cast PMMA rods with a hemispherical stagnation tip, flames survived down to about 13.5% oxygen (the minimum of the flammability boundary at stretch rate 8 to 12 per s), significantly lower than the 15.4% oxygen upward flame spread limit observed in normal gravity with an additional 4 cm/s forced flow.
quote: The minimum O2 concentration of 13.5 percent O2 at a of 8 to 12 s–1 is significantly lower than the observed upward flame spread limit of 15.4 percent O2 (in normal gravity with an additional 4-cm/s forced flow (Ref. 23)), indicating the material remains flammable under the weak ventilation only obtainable in microgravity.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report (NASA/TM-20210011385)
source_authors: Sandra L. Olson; Paul V. Ferkul; Subrata Bhattacharjee; Fletcher J. Miller; Carlos Fernandez-Pello; Shmuel Link; James S. T'ien; Indrek Wichman
source_org: NASA Glenn Research Center

material: Cast PMMA cylindrical rods with hemispherical stagnation tip, radii 0.318 cm (primary), 0.476 cm and 0.635 cm, clear; plus two black rods of r = 0.318 cm

conditions.pressure_text: Not stated for the Ch. 6 rod tests (the 250 L Microgravity Science Glovebox volume held ISS air diluted with N2). Another BASS-II chapter (Ch. 2, report p. 38) logs 99.2 to 99.5 kPa total pressure for its own tests. No pressure is given for the 15.4% 1-g comparison point.
conditions.flow_text: Stretch rate a = 8 to 12 per s at the minimum (rod-size adjusted); forced flows 0 to 55 cm/s in the experiment; the 1-g comparison point has a 4 cm/s added forced flow

limits: One material and geometry (hemispherical tip of a rod, concurrent flow). 13.5% O2 is the minimum of a U-shaped boundary that exists only in a narrow weak-flow window; away from it the limit is higher. The same chapter puts the ignition limit higher (about 14.5% O2), so a cold item must still be ignited. The 15.4% comparison is a 1-g value for PMMA rods, not a measurement on a cargo item. Says nothing about other materials or thicknesses. The 15.4% comparison value comes from the report's Ref. 23, which was not opened.
usefulness: (a)(c) Concrete number for how much lower the oxygen limit of a common plastic can be in microgravity with spacecraft-like weak ventilation (about 2 points of O2 for PMMA), and that the effect needs the right flow window.
verifier_note: Quote found exactly; located on report p. 76 = PDF p. 84 (checked by page). Context supports the claim. Changes: claim names the geometry and the boundary point it comes from; material corrected to the radii and rod types the text lists (the previous 'per Fig. 6.3' source is not needed, the text states 0.318, 0.476, 0.635 cm); pressure text no longer implies the 99.2-99.5 kPa applies to these rods, because the chapter that logs it is a different experiment. Verified in the same chapter: ignition limit about 14.5% O2, flames survived to 13.6% when ignited at higher O2, flows 0 to 55 cm/s, 'Concurrent-flow flame spread tests burned an axisymmetric cylindrical PMMA rod'.

claim: NASA's opposed-flow flammability map for a cellulose fuel shows a limiting oxygen index of 16.5% O2 on Earth, but at flows of the order of spacecraft ventilation (5 to 20 cm/s) flames can be sustained even at 14% O2.
quote: In the opposed flow flame spread flammability map for a cellulose fuel, the LOI, or limiting oxygen index on Earth in opposed flow is 16.5% O2. However, if the flow is on the order of spacecraft ventilation (5-20 cm/s), flames can be sustained even at 14 % O2.

claim: In ISS tests on 4 cm PMMA spheres at about 1.03 to 1.07 atm, a flame lasted until oxygen fell to 13.5% at an intermediate flow of 11.5 cm/s, but went out at 20.8% oxygen at 0.44 cm/s and at 15.0% oxygen at 34.3 cm/s.

source_authors: Chengyao Li; James S. T'ien; Paul V. Ferkul; Sandra L. Olson; Michael C. Johnston

limits: Five tests only. Oxygen falls gradually as the sample burns while flow is held constant, so the O2 values are at extinction of an already established flame, not ignition limits. One material and a sphere geometry. Extinction at 0.44 cm/s was by quenching, at 34 cm/s by blowoff, at 11.5 cm/s at the junction of the two. No claim for other thicknesses or materials.
usefulness: (c) Shows the same U-shaped flow dependence for a thick plastic: lowest survivable oxygen at moderate low flow, much higher oxygen needed at near-zero flow. Supports airflow speed as a risk dial.
verifier_note: Quote found exactly (three rows of Table 1, PDF p. 3). Column mapping checked against the table header and footnotes: Flow (cm/s) | Reynolds number | strain rate (1/s) | O2 (%) at extinction | p (atm) | conductive heat loss. Case 2 = blowoff 34.28 cm/s, 14.99% O2, 1.06 atm; case 3 = intermediate 11.50 cm/s, 13.54% O2, 1.07 atm; case 4 = quenching 0.44 cm/s, 20.77% O2, 1.03 atm. Abstract confirms 4-cm PMMA spheres, 0.2 to 80 cm/s, oxygen 13 to 28% in one atmosphere, extinction by natural oxygen depletion; 6.35 mm support tube and CIR/SoFIE insert confirmed in the text. NTRS record: Combustion Institute 40th International Symposium, Milan, July 2024.

limits: One test, at raised oxygen and reduced pressure (an exploration-type atmosphere, not ISS air). The authors cannot tell whether surviving flamelets, glowing char embers or both kept the fire going during the 70 s; they say a surviving flamelet is likely. The paper then concludes that for thinner materials flames can persist for an extended period without forced flow, and (Saffire V-3 and V-4 PMMA) that after a 300 s cool-down at 5 cm/s the flame went out immediately when the fan stopped. The text gives both 'initial 300 seconds' and 'approximately 280 seconds' for when the fan went off.
usefulness: (b)(c) Evidence that stopping airflow does not reliably stop a thin-fabric fire when oxygen is raised and pressure lowered, as in some habitat atmospheres.

claim: NASA estimated that on the Moon or Mars (0.17 g and 0.38 g) buoyant flows exceed 20 cm/s, so a flow-assisted concurrent flame can spread alongside any opposed-flow flame.
quote: On the Moon or Mars (0.17g and 0.38 g, respectively), where buoyant flows will be greater than 20 cm/s, the concurrent flame spread will be viable simultaneously with any opposed flow flame.

limits: A 2004 estimate, not a measurement. The paper cites KC-135 aircraft tests showing faster concurrent burning in partial gravity, which were not opened. Ruff (2021) uses 0.16 g and about 0.2 m/s buoyant velocity for the Moon.
usefulness: (c) Ties the gravity level to the airflow regime: at lunar and Martian gravity buoyancy supplies enough flow to support the faster flow-assisted flame.
